jurisdiction.name: South Africa
jurisdiction.overview: Nationally published records appear separately from applicable EU-level records. The landscape, historical relationships and legal applicability remain under document-level review.

narrative.summary: South Africa has no AI-specific law. AI is governed through the Protection of Personal Information Act's rule on automated decision-making (s.71) and the communications department's non-binding AI Policy Framework issued for comment in October 2024; its 2026 draft successor, the Draft National AI Policy, was withdrawn in June 2026. A sector layer is growing: the financial supervisors' report on AI in the financial sector, the Health Professions Council's 2025 ethical guidelines on AI for health practitioners, and Competition Commission remedies of November 2025 on generative AI and news content.
lead_institutions: Department of Communications and Digital Technologies
narrative.review_notes: This review was first completed on 12 October 2026 and redone in a longer pass on 13 October 2026, covering the Government Gazette, Parliament, the government, each ministry and each sector regulator. The medicines regulator's and the higher-education council's websites and Parliament's bill pages could not be accessed. A revised national AI policy, the medicines regulator's AI/ML device guidance, election AI-labelling rules and the judiciary's draft AI policy are tracked as leads.

instruments.official_title: Protection of Personal Information Act, 2013 (Act No. 4 of 2013)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of the Republic of South Africa (assented to by the President; published by The Presidency, Government Notice 912, Government Gazette No. 37067)
instruments.current_status: In force. Section 115 commencement: Proclamation R.21 of 2020 (Government Gazette No. 43461, 22 June 2020) brought sections 2-38, 55-109 (including section 71 on automated decision making), 111 and 114(1)-(3) into force on 1 July 2020, and sections 110 and 114(4) on 30 June 2021; section 114(1) gave a one-year transition to comply. Section 1, Part A of Chapter 5 and sections 112-113 had commenced earlier (11 April 2014). Enforced by the Information Regulator.
instruments.summary: South Africa's general data protection law: it sets eight conditions for lawful processing of personal information, regulates direct marketing, transborder flows and special personal information, and establishes the Information Regulator. Section 71 provides that a data subject may not be subject to a decision with legal consequences or substantial effect based solely on automated processing intended to profile the person (e.g. work performance, creditworthiness, health, conduct), unless the decision is linked to a contract with appropriate safeguards or governed by a law or code with such measures; the safeguards must let the person make representations and give sufficient information about the underlying logic of the processing.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Binding rules on automated decision-making and profiling (s.71) and on personal data used to train and run AI systems; the main binding AI-relevant law in South Africa.
instruments.evidence_reference: Re-checked 2026-10-13: curl (browser user agent, --max-time 60) of the Government Gazette No. 37067 PDF on gov.za (Act text incl. section 71 read with pdftotext); commencement read from Proclamation R.21 of 2020, Government Gazette No. 43461 (https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202006/43461rg11136pr21.pdf, linked from the gov.za notice page). The 11 April 2014 date for section 1, Part A of Chapter 5 and sections 112-113 is the gov.za notice listing title; that proclamation was not opened.

instruments.summary: Report of the Presidential Commission on the 4th Industrial Revolution, published by the Minister of Communications and Digital Technologies under the Commission's terms of reference (Gazette No. 42388 of 9 April 2019). It diagnoses South Africa's readiness for 4IR technologies, including artificial intelligence, and makes key recommendations such as investing in human capacity, building digital infrastructure, establishing an AI institute (a 'creative AI, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain and Cybersecurity' institute), securing government and citizens' data and updating regulation.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: First government-commissioned national roadmap that framed AI as a priority and recommended an AI institute; precursor to the national AI policy process.

instruments.official_title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework
instruments.english_title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework (Towards the Development of South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy)
instruments.issuing_authority: Department of Communications and Digital Technologies
instruments.current_status: Issued by DCDT for public input (comments to DCDT by 17h00 on Friday 29 November 2024); the cover is dated October 2024 and the DCDT download page lists it with the date 25 October 2024. The Draft South Africa National AI Policy (Gazette No. 54477, 10 April 2026) refers to it as the 'National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework of August 2024' that received 32 submissions; the date printed on the Framework itself (October 2024) is recorded. That draft policy was withdrawn (Notice 3978 of 2026, Gazette 54840, 12 June 2026), so this Framework remains the latest published national AI policy document; no final national AI policy has been adopted.
instruments.summary: Twenty-page DCDT framework described as the first step towards a National AI Policy, released for public comment. It sets out South Africa's policy-making life cycle, the rationale for an AI policy, a 'futures triangle' problem analysis, and nine strategic pillars: talent and capacity development, digital infrastructure, research and innovation, public sector implementation (including guidelines for ethical AI in government), ethical AI guidelines, privacy and data protection, safety and security, transparency and explainability, and fairness and bias mitigation. It is non-binding and invites stakeholder inputs to shape the eventual policy.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Latest published national AI policy document after the 2026 draft policy was withdrawn; basis for the 2026 draft.

instruments.official_title: Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy
instruments.english_title: Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy (General Notice 3880 of 2026)
instruments.issuing_authority: Minister of Communications and Digital Technologies (Department of Communications and Digital Technologies); approved by Cabinet on 25 March 2026
instruments.current_status: Published for 60 days' public comment (deadline 10 June 2026) in Government Gazette No. 54477 of 10 April 2026 (notice signed 9 April 2026). Parliament's Portfolio Committee on Communications and Digital Technologies announced on 25 May 2026 a briefing (26 May 2026) on the circumstances of the withdrawal, citing allegations that parts of the document contained AI-generated content with unverifiable sources. Cabinet approved the withdrawal at its meeting of 3 June 2026 so that the policy can be reworked. Formally withdrawn in its entirety by General Notice 3978 of 2026 (Gazette No. 54840, 12 June 2026; signed 4 June 2026), effective from publication. No replacement draft was found on official sites as of 2026-10-13.
instruments.summary: Cabinet-approved draft national AI policy published by the Minister of Communications and Digital Technologies for public comment under section 85(2)(b) of the Constitution. It set out strategic pillars and a staged implementation (finalise the policy and draft rules for unacceptable risks in 2025/26; guidelines and high-risk requirements in 2026/27) and proposed new institutions including a National AI Commission/Office, an AI Ethics Board, an AI Regulatory Authority, an AI Ombudsperson Office, an AI Insurance Superfund and a National AI Safety Institute, with ICASA repositioned and a National AI Regulatory Forum coordinating the Information Regulator, Competition Commission, SARB, FSCA and others. It was withdrawn before finalisation.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: South Africa's first gazetted national AI policy draft; withdrawn, kept for the timeline.

instruments.english_title: Artificial Intelligence in the South African Financial Sector
instruments.issuing_authority: Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA) and Prudential Authority (PA, South African Reserve Bank)
instruments.current_status: Published jointly on 24 November 2025 (date of the FSCA/PA press release; the report cover says November 2025) on the SARB Prudential Authority publications page, with a databook and survey questionnaire. Non-binding; it envisages future sector-wide guidance on ethical and responsible AI.
instruments.summary: Joint FSCA and Prudential Authority report giving the first overview of AI, machine learning and generative AI adoption in South African financial institutions, based on a 2024 survey of banks, insurers, investment managers and payment providers. It reviews international regulatory approaches, use cases, risks (privacy, bias, explainability, systemic risk) and governance and ethics considerations, and sets out lessons: explainability methods, board-level AI governance and model risk management, disclosure of AI in consumer-impacting decisions such as credit and insurance pricing, coordination with the Information Regulator on POPIA, and planned sector-wide guidance.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Financial supervisors' first AI-specific publication and signal of forthcoming sector guidance.

instruments.official_title: Guidelines for Good Practice in the Health Professions: Ethical Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (Booklet 20)
instruments.english_title: Ethical Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (HPCSA Booklet 20)
instruments.issuing_authority: Health Professions Council of South Africa
instruments.current_status: Booklet dated September 2025 (Pretoria). The HPCSA's Corporate Affairs announced on its blog that the revised Booklet 20 was published alongside revised Booklet 7 and is available on the HPCSA website (post dated 4 December 2025). The guidelines apply to all practitioners registered with the HPCSA and are the standard against which professional conduct is evaluated.
instruments.summary: Ethical guidelines of the statutory health professions regulator on the use of AI by all practitioners registered under the Health Professions Act 56 of 1974. Practitioners must assess that AI tools are fit for purpose, valid, reliable and explainable, disclose to patients whether a tool learns from training data or is a continuous learning system, use only AI validated for reliability and cultural appropriateness, and ensure AI embedded in medical devices complies with SAHPRA requirements. Practitioners remain accountable for harms from AI use and keep the final clinical decision; the booklet also covers equity and transparency, safety and quality, CPD, and data privacy under POPIA.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: First AI-specific professional conduct guidelines for health practitioners in South Africa.

instruments.official_title: Media and Digital Platforms Market Inquiry (MDPMI) Final Report, Annexure 8: Remedial Actions
metadata_gaps: effective_date (gazette publication under s.43E(1) not located)
instruments.english_title: Media and Digital Platforms Market Inquiry Final Report: Remedial Actions (Annexure 8)
instruments.issuing_authority: Competition Commission of South Africa (Media and Digital Platforms Market Inquiry, initiated under section 43B(1)(a) of the Competition Act 89 of 1998)
instruments.current_status: Final report and remedial actions released on 13 November 2025 (Commission media statement of that date; Annexure 8 cover dated November 2025). Remedial actions are made under section 43D(1) of the Competition Act; several were agreed by the firms concerned. They take effect on the 'Effective Date', defined as the date the final report and decision is published in the Government Gazette under section 43E(1); that gazette notice was not located in this review, so effective_date is left open. Most remedies run for five years (Google) or two years (OpenAI training).
instruments.summary: Remedial actions imposed after the Competition Commission's market inquiry into media and digital platforms, addressed to Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, TikTok and X/xAI. AI-specific measures include: Google must give South African publishers parity with EU publishers in controlling how their content appears in AI Overviews in Search and fund AI innovation and training for news publishers; Microsoft's remedies cover content monetisation and opt-outs for AI; OpenAI must give South African news publishers biannual training on opt-out controls for use of their content in training large language models and grounding AI-generated responses. Non-compliance can be enforced through notices and applications to the Competition Tribunal.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: First binding competition remedies in South Africa that address generative AI use of news content and publisher opt-outs.

instruments.english_title: South Africa's Artificial Intelligence (AI) Planning: Adoption of AI by Government (draft National AI Plan, discussion document for the National AI Government Summit)
instruments.issuing_authority: Department of Communications and Digital Technologies (prepared by the Chief Directorate ICT Forecasting and Modelling; foreword by Minister Mondli Gungubele)
instruments.current_status: Draft discussion document dated October 2023, presented as the draft National AI Plan at the National AI Government Summit convened by the Minister (keynote 5 April 2024). The DCDT page describes it as a pre-policy process to collate inputs before the plan goes through the Cabinet system for public comment. Superseded in practice by the National AI Policy Framework (October 2024) and the Draft National AI Policy (2026, withdrawn); the document's disclaimer says it is a draft for discussion, not for publication.
instruments.summary: Fifty-three-page DCDT discussion document setting out a draft national AI plan focused on government adoption of AI. It reviews global AI discourse and South Africa's landscape (building on the PC4IR report and the AI Institute of South Africa), proposes priority focus areas and enablers, ethical considerations, a regulatory approach and an AI and data governance structure, and a timeline for plan adoption.

instruments.official_title: Communication to Stakeholders MD08-2025/2026: Regulatory Requirements of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) Enabled Medical Devices
instruments.english_title: SAHPRA Communication MD08-2025/2026: Regulatory Requirements of AI/ML-Enabled Medical Devices
instruments.issuing_authority: South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA)
instruments.current_status: Issued 26 September 2025 as SAHPRA Communication to Stakeholders, Issue No. MD08-2025/2026. The text states that formal regulatory pathways for AI/ML-enabled medical devices are yet to be developed and that SAHPRA has not yet called up medical devices for product registration; establishment licensing under s.22C of the Medicines and Related Substances Act 101 of 1965 applies. It is a communication to industry, not a regulation; no commencement clause.
instruments.summary: SAHPRA's communication to industry setting out its position on AI/ML-enabled medical devices and IVDs, including software as a medical device. It states that such devices need SAHPRA authorisation and a medical device establishment licence, are classified under the existing four-class risk system, and must meet existing essential principles, ISO 13485 quality management and clinical-evidence requirements, with Class C and D devices also needing approval from a reference regulator. It sets guiding principles (patient safety, transparency and explainability, cybersecurity and POPIA privacy, performance monitoring, clinical evaluation), post-market surveillance and incident-reporting expectations, and interim change-control expectations for adaptive algorithms.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Health products regulator's guidance on AI/ML-enabled medical devices.

leads.english_title: Information Regulator AI or automated decision-making guidance

Re-check inforegulator.org.za (site intermittently unreachable) before recording anything.

leads.title: Electoral Commission draft amendments to the Electoral Code (digital campaigning, labelling of AI-generated content) for the 2026 local government elections
leads.english_title: IEC draft digital campaigning rules (AI labelling, deepfakes, bots)
leads.note: Reported as published on 30 June 2026 for comment; would require labelling of AI-generated campaign material and discourage deepfakes and bots. Official text not found on elections.org.za (script-rendered pages) or gov.za on 2026-10-13. Find the gazette notice or IEC document and record as consultation_draft (or adopted rules). Update 2026-10-18: the Electoral Commission's statement on gov.za says it promulgated the final 'Electoral Code of Conduct Countering Disinformation in the Local Government Elections' on 4 September 2026 under s.88(a) of the Municipal Electoral Act 27 of 2000, effective immediately until the declaration of results, requiring clear labelling of AI-generated (synthetic) content. The code text was not found on elections.org.za or gov.za, so it stays a lead until the text is read.

leads.title: Guidance Note on the Processing of Personal Information of Voters, and the Countering of Misinformation and Disinformation during Elections (May 2024)

leads.note: Official PDF read 2026-10-13 (inforegulator.org.za guidance-notes page). Advisory note dated May 2024; AI content is limited to paras 10.3 and 12.3 (generative AI voice/image misuse; parties' commitments should provide for monitoring deep fakes and AI-generated content). Held as a lead because AI is only a small part of the note; promote if the lead reviewer treats para 12.3 as AI expectations.
